opus-5.5.text:
I think people often over-attribute the differences between models to raw capability, as if there's one ladder and every lab is just at a different rung. In my experience, a lot of what you see is actually the result of deliberate choices about what to prioritize.

When you train a frontier model, you have a finite budget: compute, data, researcher time, and especially attention in post-training. Every team has to decide what to optimize. Is it coding? Long-horizon agentic tasks? Math and reasoning? Creative writing, conversational warmth, safety behavior? Each of those needs its own data, its own environments, its own evaluation. You can't push all of them equally hard at the same time. So when one model seems much better at, say, agentic coding and another feels more natural to talk to, that often reflects where each team put its effort, not that one is fundamentally "smarter."

Capability still matters, of course. Pretraining scale, data quality, and the base model's general reasoning set a ceiling. If the base is weaker, no amount of focused post-training will fully close the gap. But between the top few labs, the base models are closer than people think, and the visible differences come much more from post-training priorities, reward design, and which environments the RL was run on.

There's also a subtler point. Prioritization isn't neutral, because it shapes the model's habits. If you train heavily on verifiable tasks like math or code, where there's a clear right answer, the model learns to be persistent, to check its work, to keep going. That can transfer to other areas, but it can also make the model feel a bit mechanical in open-ended conversation. If you emphasize human preference, you might get something more pleasant but less rigorous. So the priorities you set end up becoming part of the model's personality.

My view is that, going forward, the competition will increasingly be about taste: deciding which problems are worth solving and building the right environments and evaluations for them. Raw capability will keep improving across the board, but what will distinguish a model is what its builders chose to care about.

r001.rationale: The response says deliberate priorities explain much of the visible differences among models, but does not place that claim in the past as the criterion requires.

r002.rationale: It explains that teams choose what to optimize and devote effort, data, environments, and evaluations to those capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people tend to over-attribute the differences between models to raw capability, as if there's one scalar of "how smart" and labs are just at different points on it. In my experience, a lot of what you actually feel when you use different models comes from deliberate choices about what to prioritize.

Take something like agentic behavior. Whether a model is good at taking actions, using tools, recovering from errors — that's not something that just falls out of scaling. Someone decided that this matters, built the environments, built the evaluations, and spent compute on it. Another lab might have decided that math and competition problems were the thing to push, or that conversational quality was the thing. The underlying pretraining might be fairly comparable, but the post-training reflects a worldview about what the model is for.

I actually think the "capability gap" between frontier labs is smaller than it looks from the outside, and the "priority gap" is bigger. When you see a model that's noticeably better at, say, long-horizon coding tasks, the question I ask is not "how did they get a smarter model" but "what did they choose to measure, and what did they choose to give up." Because there are always tradeoffs. If you optimize hard for being a careful, reliable agent, you might lose some of the playfulness or the willingness to speculate that makes a model fun to talk to. If you optimize for benchmark scores, you might get something that's impressive on paper but awkward in actual use.

That said, I don't want to say capability doesn't matter — it obviously does. The way I'd put it is that capability sets the ceiling, and priorities determine where under that ceiling you actually end up. And at this moment in the field, we're in a period where the ceiling is high enough that priorities are doing a lot of the work in differentiating what people experience. That's also what makes it interesting from a research perspective: the question of "what should we want the model to be good at" is now at least as important as "how do we make it better," and it's a question that doesn't have a purely technical answer.

r001.rationale: The response says priorities currently explain much of the differences among models, but does not state that they accounted for most differences in the past.

r002.rationale: It explains that when a lab prioritizes a capability, it builds environments and evaluations and spends compute to develop it.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions: what a model can do, and what it has been trained to prioritize. Those can look very similar from the outside. If one model gives a short answer and another spends a long time exploring alternatives, you might conclude that the second model is more capable. But perhaps the first model is prioritizing speed or conciseness. The behavior alone doesn’t tell you which explanation is right.

At the same time, prioritizing something doesn’t automatically give you the capability to do it. You can train a model to try to be careful, but it still needs to recognize mistakes and know how to correct them. Otherwise, you might just get a longer answer with the same error.

So I would try to separate those factors: under comparable instructions and resource constraints, can the model actually solve the problem? And across different situations, does it make good decisions about when to answer immediately, when to think more, and when to ask for clarification? The first is about capability; the second is about how that capability gets used. For a useful system, you need both.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes priorities from capability but does not state that priorities explained most model differences in the past.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that prioritizing a capability leads developers to invest more effort in developing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things that can look similar from the outside. One is whether a model can do something; the other is whether it tends to do it. A model might be capable of giving a very detailed answer, but its training encourages it to be concise. Or it might be capable of exploring several possible solutions, but the product prioritizes a quick response.

So when we compare models, the behavior we observe reflects both capability and choices about how to use that capability. Those choices can involve post-training, system instructions, or how much computation you allow at inference time. A difference in the default answer doesn’t necessarily mean a difference in the underlying ceiling.

But priorities and capability aren’t completely separate, either. If you consistently prioritize a particular kind of task during training, you may actually become better at it. The useful question is: under comparable conditions, can the model do the task reliably? And then, separately, is that the behavior its developers have chosen to make the default?

r001.rationale: The response says observed differences reflect both capability and choices, but does not state that deliberate priorities accounted for most model differences in the past.

r002.rationale: It says prioritizing a task during training may make a model better at it, but does not explain that this priority leads developers to invest more effort in that capability.
